title: Autonomic dysfunction in Parkinson’s disease – new diagnostic methods and clinical correlates
summary:
In Parkinson’s disease, patients may experience not only movement problems but also symptoms affecting the autonomic nervous system, such as a significant drop in blood pressure when standing up. This study aims to investigate whether the function of a specific area of the brain, called the locus coeruleus, is related to these symptoms.

A special eye-tracking method will be used to measure changes in pupil size in response to different stimuli. In addition, blood pressure and heart rate will be measured, and symptoms as well as possible changes in movement, thinking, and other non-motor functions will be assessed.

The aim of the study is to better understand the relationship between autonomic dysfunction, locus coeruleus function, and other symptoms of Parkinson’s disease. In the long term, the findings may help improve the recognition and understanding of autonomic dysfunction in Parkinson’s disease.

interventions.name: The aim of the study is to indirectly assess the function of the locus coeruleus (LC) noradrenergic system in patients with Parkinson’s disease using pupillometry (EyeLink 1000) and to investigate its association with clinical features of the disease. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Clinically established diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease according to the Movement Disorder Society (MDS) criteria, from Hoehn and Yahr stage 1 onwards.
Capacity to provide informed consent and adequate cognitive function, defined as a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score >16 points.
German as the participant’s native language or sufficient proficiency in German to understand the study procedures and provide informed consent.
Exclusion criteria:
Clinically relevant pre-existing cardiovascular disease.
Manifest dementia or other neurological or psychiatric disorders (excluding Parkinson’s disease) that may interfere with study assessments or impair the capacity to provide informed consent.
Diseases or medications that substantially affect autonomic regulation or may confound the study results (with the exception of Parkinson’s disease medication).
Inability to stand safely due to an increased risk of falling during the Schellong test.
Relevant ocular diseases, including previous eye surgery, glaucoma, pseudoexfoliation syndrome involving the pupillary margin or lens, corneal disease, non-spherical pupils, or clinically relevant anisocoria.
Diabetes mellitus.
Multifocal contact lenses, reflective glasses, or glasses with extensive reflective/decorative elements. If these can be removed and visual acuity remains sufficient to fixate on the fixation cross, participants may be included, and the measurements will be performed without the visual aid.
